new_statements.quote: Stress is normally initial in Yagara, as in Duuŋidjawu (Kite and Wurm 2004, 22) and Yugambeh-Bandjalang (Sharpe 1998, 18). Watson notices the initial stress pattern in Yagara (1943, 8), which is confirmed by the Yagara words in Wurm's recording (Wurm 1960). [...] Though stress is generally initial, long vowels in the second syllable attract stress, as occurs in the nearby Yugambeh-Bandjalang and Badjala languages (Sharpe 1998, 14; Bell 2003, 24). For example, Meston (1867–1960) places a stress mark over the second syllable of his notations of magiiba 'friend' and jaraagil 'frog', which would otherwise have initial stress. [...] Compounded words keep the stress patterns of the component words.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the first syllable of the word; if the second syllable has a long vowel (at most one long vowel per morpheme) it takes the stress instead; compounds retain the stress of each member (e.g. first and third syllables stressed in bina-wali 'deaf', Guji-mulu 'Coochiemudlo'). An alternative catalog reading is fixed: initial syllable with a vowel-length exception; the source's own headline is 'Stress is normally initial'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such. The compound examples show two stressed syllables (first and third), i.e. each component keeps its initial stress. Holmer 1983 (survey-wide, p. 205) speaks of secondary stress on alternate syllables after a stressed second syllable in long words, but that is a generalisation over all languages of his survey, not a Yagara-specific statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowel in the second syllable attracts stress (magiiba 'friend', jaraagil 'frog', diyiin 'today', waliinggara 'old woman'). Older sources disagree with one another: Lauterer 1895:619 (Yerongpan dialect) 'The accent is mostly on the penultimate'; Watson 1943:8 'Accent is generally on the first syllable and, to a lesser degree, on the third' but with a p. 9 disclaimer that his Yugarabul accentuation is not first-hand; Holmer 1983:5 'Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey', with a tendency toward second-syllable prominence in longer words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, inferred for an extinct language from 19th-20th-century transcriptions (stress marks in Meston's manuscripts, prestopped spellings in Ridley and Watkins) and from Wurm's 1960 AIATSIS recording; evidence is isolated words, placenames and compounds, not phrasal prosody. No living-speaker instrumental evidence exists.
new_statements.identity_note: Sullivan & Harward-Nalder 2024 treat 'Yagara' as one language with the dialects Durubal/Turrbal (Brisbane), Yerongpan (Lauterer's 'Yaggara'), and the saltwater dialects Jandai and Munjan (= Holmer's 'Nunagal', North Stradbroke Island); this matches Glottolog's language-level yaga1256 'Yagara-Jandai' (no dialect children on the downloaded page; AIATSIS E23 Yagara, E86 Turrbal, E24 Jandai). The stress section is stated for Yagara as a whole; the supporting evidence comes from mainland (Ridley, Meston, Wurm) and island (Watkins) transcriptions. Lauterer 1895's penultimate-accent remark is for the Yerongpan dialect only; Holmer 1983's material is the Munjan/Nunagal dialect.

sources.note: Part 1 §1.3.6 'Stress', pp. 38-39: stress is normally initial (supported by Watson 1943:8, Wurm's 1960 recording and prestopping after stressed short vowels in Ridley's spellings); long vowels in the second syllable attract stress (magiiba, jaraagil, diyiin, waliinggara); compounds keep the stress of each component (first and third syllables stressed in bina-wali, Guji-mulu). §1.3.4: unstressed vowels centralise (e, o as unstressed allophones).

sources.citation: Watson, F. J. 1943 [1944]. Vocabularies of four representative tribes of South Eastern Queensland; with grammatical notes thereof and some notes on manners and customs. Supplement to the Journal of the Royal Geographical Society of Australasia (Queensland) 48(34). Brisbane.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'Notes on grammar', p. 8: 'Accent is generally on the first syllable and, to a lesser degree, on the third. There are, however, some exceptions to this rule. When the first syllable of a word ends with r the preceding vowel is sometimes obscured, and the letter r stressed.. kuri'man.. Buri'mpa.' Statement covers all four languages; p. 9 disclaims first-hand knowledge for Yugarabul: 'The accentuation of word syllables in the Yugarabul vocabulary herewith is not recorded by the personal knowledge of the compiler, but on general principles of aboriginal practice.'

sources.note: Part I §2.9, p. 5 (survey-wide): 'Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length'; Part II §2.11 p. 178 and p. 205 repeat this with 'secondary stress appearing on subsequent alternate syllables'. The Nunagal (Stradbroke Island Yagara = Munjan dialect) chapter, Part III pp. 392-412, contains no stress statement of its own; §9.6 p. 413 ('Stress is.. not distinctive') is in the Manandjali (Yugambeh) chapter, not Yagara.
